title: SpaceX Is Buying Airwaves to Take On the Wireless Carriers. Is the Stock a Buy?

Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool

TMUS

Trading disclosure

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) agreed on Oct. 8 to buy Grain Management's nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz spectrum. The rocket and satellite company says the airwaves will help its Starlink Mobile service reach phones indoors. SpaceX didn't disclose terms, but The Wall Street Journal put the price at around $8 billion in cash.

Investors in the big wireless carriers took the news hard. Shares of T-Mobile US, Verizon, and AT&T each dropped over 10% the next day.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

SpaceX stock, though, hardly moved on the news, and it's dipped since. Shares trade near $146 as I write. That puts them about 31% under the record $211.39 close on June 16 and only about 8% over the $135 price set in SpaceX's IPO.

So, does SpaceX's move into the carriers' business make the stock a buy?

Image source: Getty Images.

SpaceX is paying to reach phones indoors

The deal covers up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band. SpaceX said it addresses one of the main remaining technical gaps for Starlink Mobile, as a low-band signal like this can go through walls. And the company said most existing phones already support the band.

That same week, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cleared SpaceX to launch 15,000 next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites. The Grain purchase itself still needs FCC approval.

Grain just recently bought the airwaves from T-Mobile, in a deal that closed in August, paying $2.9 billion in cash and its own 600 MHz licenses. This makes a direct comparison hard, but the reported price is well over the cash Grain paid.

The purchase comes on top of a bigger one, too. SpaceX is buying 65 MHz of spectrum from EchoStar for around $19.6 billion, a deal it expects to close at the end of November 2027.

Management's thinking on low-band spectrum also looks to have changed fast.

"You don't have to necessarily spend many billions of dollars in low-band spectrum all upfront before you deploy your system," President Gwynne Shotwell said in early August, on SpaceX's call to go over second-quarter results.

Around two months later, SpaceX reportedly agreed to spend about $8 billion on low-band spectrum. I'd say this suggests the company wants its carrier service in place earlier, even at a higher cost.

Starlink is where SpaceX makes money

Showing why SpaceX keeps investing here, revenue in its connectivity segment (which houses Starlink) rose 66% year over year to $4.3 billion in the second quarter. This was a sharp acceleration from 32% year-over-year growth in the first quarter, when the segment took in $3.3 billion. Operating income for the segment climbed 79% year over year to $1.7 billion.

Key Stats for SpaceX Stock

Price change for SpaceX stock in last 1 month: -4%

$SPCX Stock Price as of Oct. 16: $146

52-Week High: $226

$SPCX Stock Price Target: $223

What Happened?

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) has bought 800 MHz of spectrum licenses from Grain, and a source put the price at nearly $8 billion.

SpaceX called it a "critical next step" for Starlink Mobile. But a real rival to AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile will take more than airwaves.

Reuters reports that SpaceX will likely need a ground network, plus years of work and billions more.

TD Cowen estimates the build would cost more than $80 billion, which adds to what SpaceX is already spending on Starship, AI infrastructure and its Terafab chip factory.

Cities are a big hurdle. Phones have small antennas and limited power, while satellites orbit hundreds of kilometers up, much farther than a cell tower.

Anshel Sag of Moor Insights & Strategy said there are too many pitfalls for satellites to be the only source of data.

SpaceX knows this. Its plan is a hybrid one and has approval for up to 15,000 Starlink Mobile satellites and plans to add antennas on towers and rooftops.

Sag also said nobody is likely to offer SpaceX wholesale access to their networks, so it looks set to build its own.

Rivals are not worried yet. T-Mobile's CTO said the spectrum is not enough to match established networks. Verizon said airwaves are "empty" without a network to use them.

SPCX Stock Revenue, EBIT and Free Cash Flow Estimates in Billion USD (TIKR)

Management sounded confident. On the August call, Gwynne Shotwell said the company also has 65 MHz of EchoStar spectrum, which the FCC has approved.

SpaceX plans to launch its next mobile satellites next year and start service by the end of next year.

She said the EchoStar spectrum has terrestrial parts, so SpaceX will build ground hardware. Her idea is small base stations attached to Starlink dishes, which could keep costs down.

What the Market Is Telling Us About SpaceX Stock

The business behind SpaceX stock is growing fast. Revenue nearly doubled in Q2, and the company's net loss shrank. SpaceX also has $100 billion in cash after its IPO and bond sale.

But the money is going out quickly. Of the $18.4 billion in Q2 capital spending, about $15.8 billion went to AI compute.

Julie Zhu of MoffettNathanson noted that the big three carriers spent about $650 billion on networks in the decade before 2023.

She finds it hard to imagine SpaceX finishing a rival network within a decade.

SPCX Stock Street Target (TIKR)

For investors, the risk to SpaceX stock is not the technology. A mobile network would compete with Starship and AI for cash.

Key Stats for AT&T Stock

Current Price: $23.50

Target Price (Mid): ~$39

Street Target: ~$29

Potential Total Return: ~65%

Annualized IRR: ~13% / year

What Happened?

Bernstein downgraded AT&T (T) to Market Perform late on Oct. 12, cutting its target to $24 from $25 over SpaceX's push into broadband and wireless. The stock closed at $23.50 on Oct. 15.

AT&T reports Q3 results before the open on Oct. 21. It is likely the last report for CFO Pascal Desroches, who retires on Dec. 31. At a Bank of America conference on Sept. 10, he laid out where growth is supposed to come from, and the investor relations materials will show whether it is arriving.

The Lumen Gap Is Still AT&T's to Close

Desroches' clearest growth lever was the Lumen footprint. AT&T bought about 4.5 million consumer locations that were "about 25% penetrated as compared to 40%" in its own territory, and he expects "gradual improvements over the next several quarters."

On Oct. 6, AT&T agreed to fold Forged Fiber 37, the unit holding the Lumen network, and Gigapower into a wholesale fiber joint venture with GIP and CPP Investments. Key terms:

Ownership: AT&T will hold 50%, and the deal should close in the first half of 2027.

Customers: The Lumen customer relationships stay with AT&T's home internet business. At closing, the venture is expected to serve more than 1 million AT&T fiber subscribers.

Accounting: AT&T will continue reporting Forged Fiber 37 as held for sale until closing. Afterward, it will book its share of the venture's earnings rather than consolidating it.

Proceeds: The cash AT&T receives at closing will help it reach net debt of about 2.5 times adjusted EBITDA within roughly three years.

Convergence, meaning customers who buy both home internet and wireless from AT&T, is the second gauge:

Fixed wireless: Desroches said that base is already above 50%.

All internet customers: BofA analyst Michael Funk put the share also taking AT&T postpaid wireless at 42.5% after Q2, and 45% outside the Lumen footprint.

Target: Jenifer Robertson, who leads AT&T's consumer business, restated the 50% goal.

AT&T Net Debt / EBITDA (TIKR)
What Bernstein Flagged and What Q3 Has to Clear

The downgrade followed Oct. 9, when AT&T, Verizon (VZ) and T-Mobile (TMUS) fell together after SpaceX (SPCX) agreed to buy Grain Management's 800 MHz spectrum. That deal still needs FCC approval. The selloff also landed in a week when the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.36%, a 24-year high.

Bernstein also cited recent pricing moves by incumbents and expected fourth-quarter seasonality. AT&T was the last of five big wireless and cable stocks it rated Outperform, though it said Starlink is not a direct threat to AT&T's fiber. Its $24 target sits below the Street mean of around $29.

AT&T is a large US telecom provider with a market value of about $157.9b. This Mexico exit sits alongside its broader role supplying mobile and technology services across its core domestic network footprint.

4 things going right for AT&T that this headline doesn't cover.

AT&T's Mexico exit puts its fiber‑first bet under a brighter spotlight

AT&T's Narrative is built around a simple trade off. Pour money and management focus into U.S. fiber and 5G, then shrink older networks and lower returning ventures enough that recurring service revenue and cost savings carry the load.

"The key requirement is that AT&T executes on large scale fiber build out, copper retirement, and cost take out while managing device subsidies..."

See how the full story points towards a $29.05 fair value for AT&T.

The Mexico sale leans into the bullish version of that story. Management is choosing to simplify the business model and recycle capital from a non core wireless market into U.S. fiber build, where the Narrative already highlights convergence, copper retirement and recurring service revenue as the main engine. For holders who back that thesis, this looks like alignment rather than a change in direction.

The bear side does not disappear, though. Leaving Mexico trims diversification at a time when analysts already flag high debt, heavy device promotions and earnings that are forecast to decline on current estimates. If Verizon or T Mobile can scale cross border or adjacent services more effectively, AT&T's tighter geographic focus could be read as concentration risk rather than discipline.

In the end, this same transaction can either confirm a cleaner fiber led AT&T story or underline execution and concentration risks, depending on which Narrative you already believe.
